chunks.section: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation

Affiliation: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, China Datong Li Affiliation: Anhui University of Science and Technology Jinliang Ding Affiliation: Northeastern University, China Xiaojie Wang Affiliation: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, China Tiecheng Song Affiliation: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, China Zhaolong Ning Affiliation: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, China

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA .

Large-scale pre-trained models serve as general-purpose foundations for a wide range of vision and language tasks. However, as model sizes increase, full fine-tuning becomes prohibitively expensive, requiring all model parameters to be updated and a separate set of weights to be stored for each downstream task. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces this cost by freezing the pre-trained weights and optimizing only a small set of parameters [ 11 , 17 , 14 ] . Among PEFT methods, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 12 ] has been widely adopted for its low-rank parameterization of weight updates, which can be merged into the pre-trained weights without additional inference overhead. Nevertheless, LoRA often falls short of full fine-tuning. Prior work narrows this gap by modifying the update structure (DoRA [ 25 ] ), improving subspace initialization (PiSSA [ 26 ] , LoRA-GA [ 35 ] ), or correcting the factor gradients and optimizer states to better approximate full fine-tuning updates (LoRA-Pro [ 36 ] , AltLoRA [ 41 ] , LoFT [ 31 ] ). However, a fundamental local constraint remains: under factor perturbations δ ​ A \delta A and δ ​ B \delta B , the first-order weight update lies entirely in the tangent space defined by the current factors. The dense gradient component orthogonal to this space therefore cannot be captured by any first-order update, regardless of how the factor gradients are corrected at the current step.

This raises a question: how much gradient information lies outside the current tangent space? We analyze the tangent-space residual gradient across ten representative LoRA variants ( Fig. 1 ) and identify two consistent properties. First, the residual accounts for more than 85% of the total gradient energy across all methods. Second, it exhibits strong spectral concentration: the leading singular component captures more than 87% of the residual energy, while the top four capture more than 94%. These findings reveal that the current tangent space leaves substantial gradient information unexploited, yet most of this information can be recovered through a very low-rank approximation. A natural idea to exploit the residual gradient is to continually incorporate its principal directions into the trainable subspace. However, increasing the rank incurs a proportional parameter cost, whereas replacing existing factors at a fixed rank can discard accumulated adaptation information and disrupt training continuity. ReLoRA [ 20 ] , Flora [ 8 ] , and GaLore [ 47 ] also switch low-rank subspaces during training, primarily to overcome rank limitations or reduce training memory, but do not explicitly target gradient components outside the current tangent space. The key challenge is therefore to incorporate these principal residual directions within a fixed rank budget while retaining learned information, maintaining training stability, and preserving mergeability into the pre-trained weights.

To address this challenge, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch that accumulates task-specific directions as in standard LoRA and a dynamic branch that periodically absorbs principal residual directions outside the current tangent space. We prove that, under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints, the optimal update for a local quadratic model is given by the truncated SVD of the tangent-space residual gradient. Crucially, this residual inherits a factored structure from backpropagation, enabling its products with narrow matrices to be computed directly from cached input activations and output gradients. This structure allows us to construct matrix-free operators for Matrix-Free Randomized SVD, which extracts the principal residual directions via randomized SVD [ 7 ] without explicitly forming the residual gradient. To incorporate these directions while maintaining training stability, we introduce Controlled Write-back mechanism, which merges them with the current dynamic branch update, compresses the result back to the original rank, and bounds the relative change at each refresh. After training, both branches are merged into the pre-trained weights, yielding the same inference cost as standard LoRA.

We evaluate DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks: the 19 image classification tasks in VTAB-1K; object detection and instance segmentation on MS COCO; open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation (OVDG-SS) in both real-to-real and synthetic-to-real settings; eight commonsense reasoning tasks using LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B; and GLUE using DeBERTaV3-base. Under matched trainable parameter budgets, DT-LoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and its variants. On MS COCO, DT-LoRA at r = 16 r=16 achieves an average score of 46.6, exceeding LoRA at the same rank by 8.2 points and outperforming LieRA [ 29 ] , which uses twice as many trainable parameters. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA establishes new state-of-the-art results, surpassing the task-specific S 2 -Corr [ 46 ] despite being a general-purpose fine-tuning method. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify a geometric limitation of factorized LoRA: substantial gradient energy lies outside the current tangent space. Across ten representative LoRA variants, we show that this tangent-space residual exhibits strong spectral concentration, and establish that its truncated SVD yields the optimal update under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints for a local quadratic model. • We propose DT-LoRA, which partitions a fixed rank budget into Stable and Dynamic branches to incorporate principal residual directions. Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts these directions without materializing the residual gradient, while Controlled Write-back integrates them with accumulated updates and bounds the change at each refresh, enabling dynamic tangent-space adaptation without additional trainable parameters or inference overhead.

• We demonstrate the effectiveness of DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks, with consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants under matched trainable parameter budgets. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific methods and establishes new state-of-the-art results.

To avoid the memory and storage costs of full fine-tuning, PEFT freezes the pre-trained backbone and trains only a small number of parameters. Early methods can be roughly divided into three categories. The first category inserts additional trainable modules into the network, such as Adapter [ 11 ] , which adds bottleneck modules sequentially within Transformer layers, and AdaptFormer [ 3 ] , which places them in parallel with the MLP. The second category introduces learnable continuous prompts into the input or intermediate representations, such as Prompt Tuning [ 17 ] , Prefix-Tuning [ 18 ] , and VPT [ 14 ] for vision Transformers. The third category tunes only a subset of the model parameters or features, such as BitFit [ 1 ] , which fine-tunes only the bias terms, and SSF [ 21 ] , which scales and shifts the features. However, the first two categories retain extra modules or prompt tokens at inference, adding inference overhead, while the third offers limited flexibility for adaptation. In contrast, reparameterization methods such as LoRA [ 12 ] represent the weight update with low-rank matrices that can be merged into the pre-trained weights after training, balancing expressiveness and deployment efficiency. For various LoRA variants, the tangent-space residual gradient accounts for a large proportion of the gradient energy and exhibits spectral concentration. Our DT-LoRA explicitly accounts for this property, and its gradient coverage keeps increasing during training, indicating that the principal directions of the tangent-space residual gradient are effectively exploited.

Subsequent work improves LoRA mainly in three aspects. The first concerns the structure of the update and rank allocation: DoRA [ 25 ] decomposes the weight into magnitude and direction and updates the direction in low-rank form; LieRA [ 29 ] extends low-rank updates to high-dimensional parameters such as convolution kernels via the exponential map of Lie groups; AdaLoRA [ 44 ] and FlexLoRA [ 24 ] dynamically allocate the rank budget across layers according to matrix importance. The second concerns the choice of the low-rank subspace: PiSSA [ 26 ] initializes the adapter with the principal singular components of the pre-trained weights, MiLoRA [ 34 ] and SoMA [ 42 ] instead select the minor singular components to reduce interference with pre-trained knowledge, and LoRA-GA [ 35 ] aligns the initial update direction with the gradient of full fine-tuning. However, these methods determine the subspace only at the beginning of training. The third concerns the optimization process: LoRA-Pro [ 36 ] and AltLoRA [ 41 ] correct the factor gradients so that the induced equivalent gradient better approximates the full fine-tuning gradient, and LoFT [ 31 ] further aligns the moment estimates of the optimizer. Nevertheless, the first-order updates of these methods remain confined to the tangent space determined by the current factors, leaving the gradient components outside it unexploited. ReLoRA [ 20 ] , Flora [ 8 ] , and GaLore [ 47 ] switch subspaces by periodically restarting the low-rank update, resampling projections, or updating the projection subspace via the SVD of the gradient, respectively. However, they either discard the learned low-rank factors, rely on random sampling, or target full-parameter training rather than mergeable adapters, and none of them explicitly

Fig. 1 reveals two consistent phenomena across ten LoRA variants. First, the residual accounts for a substantial fraction of gradient energy: ρ \rho exceeds 85% for every method ( Fig. 1(a) ), ranging from 85.4% for PiSSA to approximately 96.9% for FlexLoRA and LieRA, with standard LoRA at 85.7%. Improved parameterizations thus do not consistently improve tangent-space gradient coverage, and some even leave more energy outside the tangent space. Second, the residual exhibits strong spectral concentration: E 1 E_{1} exceeds 87% and E 4 E_{4} exceeds 94% for all methods ( Fig. 1(b) ). The high residual energy ratio reveals substantial gradient information inaccessible to first-order updates, while its spectral concentration suggests that most of this information can be captured at a low rank. Motivated by these findings, DT-LoRA tracks the dominant residual directions during training and incorporates them through a dedicated low-rank branch.

Directly replacing the Dynamic branch with candidate direction matrix H H would discard accumulated adaptation information and could introduce abrupt changes in the model weights. We therefore introduce Controlled Write-back, which integrates H H through adaptive injection scaling, merge-and-compress, and a relative-change constraint. We evaluate DT-LoRA on vision tasks spanning image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and OVDG-SS, as well as language tasks covering commonsense reasoning and natural language understanding. We compare DT-LoRA with LoRA and representative variants across these tasks, and additionally with task-specific methods on OVDG-SS.

For image classification, we use VTAB-1K, which comprises 19 tasks across natural, specialized, and structured categories, each with 1,000 training examples. Following [ 43 , 38 ] , we adapt ViT-B/16 [ 5 ] pre-trained on ImageNet-21K. For object detection and instance segmentation, we follow LieRA [ 29 ] and fine-tune a ConvNeXt-V2-B backbone within Mask R-CNN [ 9 ] on MS COCO, using MMDetection [ 2 ] . For OVDG-SS, we adopt the benchmark protocol of S 2 -Corr [ 46 ] , training on CS-7 for real-to-real transfer or GTA-7 for synthetic-to-real transfer and reporting mIoU on two groups of unseen target domains, Dv-19 and Dv-58. We use EVA02-CLIP [ 30 ] encoders with ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/14 backbones within the CAT-Seg [ 4 ] and PCA-Seg [ 40 ] frameworks. For commonsense reasoning, we follow [ 13 ] to fine-tune LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B on Commonsense170K and evaluate on the test sets of eight tasks, including BoolQ and PIQA. For natural language understanding, we fine-tune DeBERTaV3-base [ 10 ] on eight GLUE tasks [ 33 ] . Dataset details are provided in Appendix C .

Across all tasks, DT-LoRA matches the trainable parameter budget of the LoRA baseline. For competing methods, we use the hyperparameter settings recommended in their original papers. Full task-specific configurations for DT-LoRA, including learning rates and refresh intervals, are provided in Appendix D .

As shown in Tab. 1 , DT-LoRA achieves an average accuracy of 76.2% with 0.34M trainable parameters, surpassing LoRA (75.7%), DoRA (75.8%), and FlexLoRA (76.0%) under matched parameter budgets. The largest gains occur on structured tasks involving geometric attributes, with improvements of 8.1 and 5.2 percentage points over LoRA on sNORB-Ele and sNORB-Azim, respectively. These results suggest that incorporating residual gradient directions is particularly beneficial for tasks that differ substantially from the natural-image pre-training distribution. DT-LoRA also improves performance on natural and specialized tasks, including a 1.9-point gain on CIFAR-100.

As shown in Tab. 2 , DT-LoRA at r = 16 r=16 outperforms LoRA and LieRA [ 29 ] across all reported detection and instance segmentation metrics. It achieves an All Avg. score of 46.6, exceeding LoRA and LieRA by 8.2 and 4.3 points, respectively, with detection and segmentation mAP scores of 44.1 and 40.3. DT-LoRA also surpasses LoRA r=32 and LieRA r=32 , which use twice as many trainable parameters. Doubling LoRA’s rank yields only a 0.8-point improvement in All Avg., suggesting that increasing rank alone provides limited benefits in this setting. In contrast, DT-LoRA achieves substantially larger gains within a fixed rank budget by incorporating principal residual directions outside the current tangent space. chunks.section: Open-Vocabulary Domain Generalization in Semantic Segmentation.
chunks.text: OVDG-SS requires recognizing and segmenting unseen categories in unseen target domains, jointly testing open-vocabulary recognition and cross-domain generalization. We integrate DT-LoRA into segmentation frameworks as a general-purpose fine-tuning method and compare it with LoRA, DoRA, LoRA-Pro, the domain-generalization-oriented SoMA [ 42 ] , and S 2 -Corr [ 46 ] , a method specifically designed for OVDG-SS. All LoRA-based methods use a total rank budget of r = 16 r=16 , and improvements are measured relative to the baseline of each segmentation framework. Tabs. 3 and 4 report the results. With EVA02 ViT-L/14, DT-LoRA achieves the highest average mIoU in both transfer settings. In real-to-real transfer, DT-LoRA CAT-Seg {}_{\text{CAT-Seg}} reaches 59.2 and 56.1 mIoU on Dv-19 and Dv-58, respectively, improving over CAT-Seg by 9.9 and 6.1 points, over LoRA at the same rank by 6.6 and 7.1 points, and over S 2 -Corr by 3.4 and 2.9 points. It also surpasses S 2 -Corr in synthetic-to-real transfer by 2.3 and 1.3 points on the two evaluation groups. With ViT-B/16, DT-LoRA remains the best-performing method in real-to-real transfer. In synthetic-to-real transfer, it matches S 2 -Corr on Dv-58 and trails it by 0.6 points on Dv-19, while outperforming all compared LoRA variants. Improvements also extend to PCA-Seg: DT-LoRA raises its mIoU by 2.4 and 2.6 points on Dv-19 and Dv-58 in real-to-real transfer, and by 8.6 points on Dv-58 in synthetic-to-real transfer, achieving the highest reported score of 51.8 on that evaluation group. These results demonstrate consistent improvements across encoder backbones, segmentation frameworks, and source datasets, without task-specific architectural modifications.

To assess whether the benefits extend beyond vision, we evaluate DT-LoRA on commonsense reasoning ( Tab. 5 ). On LLaMA2-7B, DT-LoRA achieves an average accuracy of 80.0% while training only 0.43% of the model parameters, exceeding LoRA [ 12 ] , which trains 0.83%, by 2.4 percentage points and slightly surpassing DoRA [ 25 ] (79.7%). On LLaMA3-8B, DT-LoRA reaches 83.3% accuracy with 0.35% trainable parameters, outperforming LoRA under the same parameter budget by 0.5 points and also surpassing MiLoRA [ 34 ] . These results demonstrate that DT-LoRA’s benefits extend to language tasks without increasing the trainable parameter budget.

On GLUE ( Tab. 6 ), DT-LoRA achieves the highest average score of 88.7, outperforming LoRA under the same parameter budget by 1.1 points and AdaLoRA, which uses more trainable parameters, by 0.6 points. It also surpasses full fine-tuning (88.3) while training less than 1% of the model parameters. The largest improvement over LoRA is observed on QQP, with a gain of 3.6 points.

We ablate three key components of DT-LoRA on OVDG-SS (real-to-real, CAT-Seg with EVA02 ViT-L/14) and MS COCO (ConvNeXt-V2-B), using the training configurations of the main experiments. w/o Dynamic Branch replaces the Dynamic branch with an additional rank-4 Stable branch, preserving the total rank budget of r = 16 r=16 and the trainable parameter count. w/ Full-Gradient Refresh extracts candidate directions from the full gradient rather than the tangent-space residual. w/o Controlled Write-back directly replaces the Dynamic branch update with the candidate update. As shown in Tab. 7 , each ablation reduces performance. Without the Dynamic branch, mIoU drops to 52.7 and 48.5 on Dv-19 and Dv-58, respectively, approaching standard LoRA performance and supporting the importance of residual-driven subspace refresh. The same trend holds on MS COCO, where the detection mAP drops from 44.1 to 36.2, close to LoRA (35.5). Full-gradient refresh also yields lower performance, suggesting that explicitly targeting directions outside the current tangent space is more effective than selecting dominant directions from the full gradient. Removing Controlled Write-back causes the largest degradation, reducing mIoU to 27.3 and 16.8 and detection mAP to 33.7, below LoRA in both cases. This result highlights the importance of integrating candidate directions with accumulated updates while controlling refresh-induced perturbations. Consistent with these findings, Fig. 1(c) shows increasing tangent-space gradient coverage during training, providing further evidence that DT-LoRA improves access to previously unexploited gradient directions. In this work, we presented DT-LoRA, a parameter-efficient adaptation method that addresses the tangent-space constraint on factorized LoRA’s first-order updates. Our analysis showed that the gradient components outside the current tangent space carry substantial energy concentrated in a few dominant directions, motivating their periodic incorporation within a fixed rank budget. DT-LoRA combines matrix-free residual direction extraction with controlled write-back to adapt the trainable subspace while limiting refresh-induced perturbations. Experiments across vision and language tasks demonstrated consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants, including new state-of-the-art results on OVDG-SS, without additional trainable parameters or inference overhead. These findings highlight the value of adapting low-rank update subspaces to previously unexploited gradient information.
